Assignment 2: Field-Level EDA & Spatial Comparison

Course: Agricultural Data Systems  |  Instructor: Clayton Young  |  Student: Oladapo Olorunfemi  |  Branch: assignment-2

1. Dataset Scope

The dataset expands from the Assignment 1 Illinois and Iowa growers into a three-grower, 30-field sample (2020–2024). Soil analysis was not performed and is not required for this assignment.

Nebraska county rationale: Hamilton County, NE sits in the densest center-pivot irrigation corridor of the Platte River valley with >85% irrigated cropland drawing from the Ogallala Aquifer — a canonical corn/soy center-pivot context.

2. Geospatial Map

Figure MAP-01: Field boundary polygons for all three growers. Each panel zooms to one grower's farm. Fields are numbered 1–10. CRS: WGS-84.

The three growers span a west–east transect from Hamilton Co., NE (~98°W) through Story Co., IA (~93.6°W) to McLean Co., IL (~88.9°W) — covering roughly 1,000 km of the US corn belt. Field shapes are slightly irregular polygons reflecting realistic PLS-based quarter-section boundaries.

3. Field Boundaries EDA

Fig FB-01: Acreage distribution histogram by grower.

Fig FB-02: Field count (solid) and total acreage (hatched) per grower.

Fig FB-03: Field acreage vs. within-grower rank (smallest→largest). Dashed lines show OLS trend; r values annotated per grower.

Findings

FB-01/02: All three growers have identical field size pools (40–150 ac, same 10-field pool), producing equal total acreage (830 ac each). This reflects the synthetic dataset design; in real data, NE center-pivot fields tend to be rounder and more uniform while IL/IA quarter-section fields vary more.
FB-03 (Correlation): Pearson r values are near zero for all three growers, confirming that within each grower's 10-field set, field rank does not predict acreage — the size pool was drawn independently of spatial position.

4. Weather EDA

Fig WX-01: Annual precipitation distribution (box + strip) per grower, 2020–2024.

Fig WX-02: Annual GDD trend (mean ± 1 SD across 10 fields) per grower.

Fig WX-03: Annual precipitation vs. annual GDD per field-year. OLS regression lines and Pearson r/p annotated per grower.

Findings

WX-01 (Precipitation): The expected precipitation gradient is visible — IL (median ~870 mm) > IA (~820 mm) > NE (~680 mm) — consistent with NOAA normal annual precipitation for these counties. The NE distribution is also tighter, reflecting the drier and more variable semi-arid climate where center-pivot irrigation compensates for deficit years.
WX-02 (GDD trend): IL fields accumulate the most annual GDD (~1,550 base-10 °C) owing to the warmer southern latitude, followed by IA (~1,200) and NE (~1,200). Year-to-year variability (shaded ±1 SD band) is moderate across all three growers, with no single extreme outlier year in the 2020–2024 window.
WX-03 (Correlation): Pearson r is near zero for all three growers (IL: r=−0.07, IA: r=−0.12, NE: r=−0.09; all p > 0.40), confirming that in this dataset annual precipitation and annual GDD are not significantly correlated within a grower. This is agronomically plausible: temperature (which drives GDD) and precipitation are driven by different synoptic patterns.

5. CDL / Cropland Data Layer EDA

Fig CDL-01: CDL crop class field counts per year by grower.

Fig CDL-02: Crop rotation heatmap — field × year for each grower.

Fig CDL-03: Field acreage vs. CDL dominant crop pixel fraction. OLS lines and Pearson r/p annotated per grower.

Findings

CDL-01 (Crop counts): IL and IA show strict binary corn–soybean rotation across all 10 fields and all 5 years (no wheat or alfalfa), while NE shows occasional Winter Wheat and Alfalfa in ~15% of field-years — reflecting the broader crop diversity typical of Nebraska's irrigated zone where a third rotation crop is economically viable.
CDL-02 (Rotation heatmap): The classic corn–soy alternating checkerboard pattern is clearly visible for IL and IA. Nebraska shows the same backbone rotation but with sporadic wheat/alfalfa disruptions, confirming that not all center-pivot fields follow a strict binary rotation.
CDL-03 (Correlation): No significant correlation between field size and CDL dominant pixel fraction was found for any grower (all p > 0.05). In a real CDL analysis, smaller fields would typically show lower purity due to edge-pixel contamination; the absence of this effect here reflects the synthetic data's uniform pixel fraction range (0.82–0.98).

7. Limitations & Assumptions

Field boundaries are synthetically generated as regular quadrilaterals with ±5% jitter. Real field polygons sourced from CLU or FSA data would show more irregular shapes, curved pivot footprints for NE, and tighter spacing between fields.
Weather data was generated from climate normal parameters (NOAA mean precipitation and temperature by state) with random noise. It is directionally accurate at the county scale but should not be treated as real historical records from NASA POWER, Daymet, or PRISM.
CDL dominant percentages (0.82–0.98) were drawn from a uniform distribution rather than from actual pixel classifications. In real CDL data, purity typically decreases with field size due to edge-pixel effects.
Soil analysis was not performed and is not required for this assignment. SSURGO-derived soil layers are available in the runtime folder from Assignment 1 but were intentionally excluded here per the assignment instructions.
